episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for the week ending Friday, July tenth, twenty-twenty-six. And here's who is innovating in higher education this week.

<break time="1.0s"/>

OpenAI this week released the GPT-5.6 model family, spanning enterprise work, coding, and scientific research, TechCrunch reported Thursday. The family arrives in three variants. OpenAI described Sol as its workhorse model, alongside Terra and Luna. The company called GPT-5.6 its strongest cybersecurity model yet, citing support for defensive activities including threat modeling, code review and patching, and blue teaming. Blue teaming, for context, involves simulating an attack on an organization's own systems to identify weaknesses before real attackers can exploit them. Alongside the model family, OpenAI released a separate workplace tool called ChatGPT Work, designed as a companion for enterprise teams. The company described it as running across desktop, web, and mobile platforms, built to assist with daily clerical tasks such as drafting documents, spreadsheets, and presentations. The GPT-5.6 release follows similar model announcements this week from SpaceXAI and Meta. The Trump administration had previously sought to restrict the rollout over concerns about potential misuse, and the models are now available across ChatGPT, Codex, and the OpenAI A.P.I.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Case Study this week, Stanford HAI reported on a biomedical A.I. agent called Biomni, built by a Stanford-led team drawing on expertise from the university's departments of Computer Science, Genetics, Pathology, Medicine, and Pediatrics, with contributions from Genentech, Arc Institute, the University of Washington, and the University of California, San Francisco. In its first nine months as an open-source project, Biomni was used by more than fifteen thousand scientists to automate one hundred thousand different scientific workflows. The platform combines large language models with more than one hundred fifty specialized bioinformatics tools and fifty-nine curated databases. Scientists interact through a chat interface, submitting open-ended research queries; the agent formulates a step-by-step plan, writes code, and executes tasks while allowing researchers to monitor and intervene at any point. In one documented case, Biomni autonomously generated and executed a ten-step analysis plan across more than four hundred fifty Excel files from thirty participants. The creators note the system still struggles with tasks requiring nuanced clinical judgment or novel experimental reasoning. In September twenty-twenty-five, the team spun the project into a commercial startup called Phylo, while keeping the codebase fully open source.

<break time="1.0s"/>

From the research front, NYU Grossman School of Medicine and NYU's Center for Data Science published findings in Nature Communications on an A.I. test that predicts breast cancer recurrence from existing tumor slides and routine clinical data. In trials involving more than thirty-five hundred patients across fifteen populations in seven countries, the test matched or outperformed a widely used genomic test. Current genomic tests can take weeks to return results and require consuming tissue samples. The A.I. test uses pathology slides already examined by pathologists, combined with data such as tumor stage, patient age, and hormone-receptor status, and could deliver results in hours. Patients classified as high risk showed a two point eight-fold higher risk of recurrence than those classified as low risk. The test also showed performance in two breast cancer types that currently have no reliable genomic test. The researchers stated that evaluation in completed randomized clinical trials is still needed before the test could guide treatment decisions. Several paper authors hold equity in Ataraxis AI, and NYU maintains financial and intellectual property interests in the company.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Also in Case Study, Pace University's Psychiatric Mental Health Nurse Practitioner Program piloted A.I.-enabled patient simulations in Fall twenty-twenty-five, according to the university's Center for Excellence in Healthcare Simulation. Under faculty leads Laura Kelly and Gabrielle Ranger-Murdock, students used A.I. avatars to conduct independent interviews with multiple patients during a single clinic day, an activity the center's director says is not possible with traditional simulation modalities. Students practiced screening instruments for anxiety, depression, and trauma, and worked on consultation skills through unfolding patient cases. In the undergraduate nursing program, educators designed a pediatrics case featuring a nonverbal child, with the A.I. encounter built around interaction with the child's mother to develop guardian communication skills. The platforms evaluate student performance using faculty-developed rubrics assessing diagnostic accuracy and empathetic communication. Not every element has worked smoothly. The center's director recalled one A.I. avatar that repeatedly addressed everyone as "honey." The center's standardized patient program continues alongside the A.I. simulations.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Investing in Innovation, New America and the Association of Community College Trustees announced on July eighth the selection of six community colleges for a work-based learning capacity-building cohort, offered through a strategic initiative backed by the U.S. National Science Foundation. The participating institutions are City Colleges of Chicago, East Central College in Missouri, Forsyth Technical Community College in North Carolina, Santa Fe College in Florida, SUNY Broome Community College in New York, and West Valley College in California. Each cohort member will undertake a comprehensive institutional self-study and strategic planning process using a toolkit developed jointly by New America and the Association of Community College Trustees. Upon completing the process, cohort members will be recognized as pilot partners when the toolkit is published for use by community colleges nationwide. NSF Assistant Director Erwin Gianchandani cited apprenticeships, internships, and work-based learning as preparation for jobs in artificial intelligence, microelectronics, biotech, and quantum technology.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to Insights and Trends, Auburn University reported this week on a survey of one thousand nine hundred forty-seven educators, trainers, and consultants across thirty-six countries, administered by Singapore's Institute for Adult Learning. The findings appear in an open-access book co-edited by Leslie Cordie, associate professor of adult education at Auburn University, and published through Taylor and Francis. Respondents largely viewed A.I. as a tool capable of improving teaching, reducing repetitive tasks, and creating new learning opportunities. Their biggest concern was not adopting the technology but receiving adequate guidance and institutional support to use it effectively. Cordie said the technology frees time for student conversations, collaboration, and deeper learning. In her courses, she asks students to experiment with A.I., question its outputs, and examine what it can and cannot do.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Also in Insights and Trends, AZ Big Media reported that Grand Canyon University, the University of Arizona, and the University of Phoenix are each embedding A.I. ethics and critical thinking across existing coursework rather than launching standalone technical programs. GCU President Brian Mueller described the institution's position as using A.I. to supplement learning, not replace it. GCU operates four discipline-specific A.I. tutoring tools across more than ninety A.I.-integrated courses, and students are required to disclose A.I. use and are graded on how well they manage it. At the University of Arizona's College of Information Science, associate professor Diana Daly teaches students to identify bias by interacting directly with A.I. systems, for example using translation prompts to surface gender bias in outputs. The college is launching an A.I. and society minor this fall. The University of Arizona has also established an Office of Responsible Artificial Intelligence.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's this week's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

leadStory.headline: OpenAI Releases GPT-5.6 Model Family and New ChatGPT Work Tool for Enterprise Teams
leadStory.summary:
OpenAI this week released the GPT-5.6 model family, spanning enterprise work, coding, and scientific research, TechCrunch reported Thursday. The family comes in three variants, with OpenAI describing Sol as its workhorse model, alongside Terra and Luna.

OpenAI called GPT-5.6 its “strongest cybersecurity model yet,” citing support for defensive activities including threat modeling, code review and patching, and blue teaming — a practice that involves simulating an attack on an organization’s own systems to identify weaknesses before real attackers can exploit them.

Alongside the model family, OpenAI released a separate workplace tool called ChatGPT Work, designed as a companion for enterprise teams. The company described it as running across desktop, web, and mobile platforms and built to assist with daily clerical tasks including drafting documents, spreadsheets, and presentations.

The GPT-5.6 release follows similar model announcements this week from SpaceXAI and Meta. TechCrunch reported the release appears aimed at rival Anthropic, which has focused on enterprise customers. The Trump administration had previously sought to restrict GPT-5.6’s rollout over concerns about potential misuse; the models are now available across ChatGPT, Codex, and the OpenAI A.P.I.

quickHits.headline: Stanford-Led Team Builds Biomedical A.I. Agent That Has Automated 100,000 Research Workflows
quickHits.summary:
In its first nine months as an open-source project, a biomedical A.I. agent called Biomni was used by more than 15,000 scientists to automate 100,000 different scientific workflows, Stanford HAI reported. The platform was built by a Stanford-led team drawing on expertise from the university's departments of Computer Science, Genetics, Pathology, Medicine, and Pediatrics, with contributions from Genentech, Arc Institute, the University of Washington, and the University of California, San Francisco.

Biomni is a cloud-based platform that combines large language models with more than 150 specialized bioinformatics tools, 59 curated databases containing protein structures, genomic variants, and literature repositories, and more than 100 software packages for molecular modeling and single-cell analysis. Scientists interact with the system through a chat interface, submitting open-ended research queries; the agent formulates a step-by-step plan, writes Python code, and executes tasks while allowing researchers to monitor and intervene at any point.

In one documented case study, Biomni autonomously generated and executed a 10-step analysis plan across 458 Excel files from 30 participants wearing continuous glucose monitors. In other cases, it analyzed large genomic datasets and designed laboratory protocols for wet-lab researchers.

The creators note Biomni still struggles with tasks requiring nuanced clinical judgment, novel experimental reasoning, or deep biological synthesis. In September 2025, the team spun the project into a commercial startup called Phylo, while keeping the codebase fully open source. An Academic Lab Program is available to universities.

quickHits.headline: NYU Researchers Build A.I. Test That Predicts Breast Cancer Recurrence Faster and Cheaper Than Genomic Testing
quickHits.summary: An A.I. test that predicts breast cancer recurrence from existing tumor slides and routine clinical data matched or outperformed a widely used genomic test in trials involving more than 3,500 patients, according to a paper published in Nature Communications by researchers at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and NYU's Center for Data Science. Current genomic tests can take weeks to return results, require consuming tissue samples that cannot be used for future testing, and carry significant cost. The A.I. test, by contrast, uses pathology slides already examined by pathologists — combined with data such as tumor stage, patient age, and hormone-receptor status — and could deliver results in hours. The model was developed and evaluated across 15 patient populations in seven countries. In the evaluation cohort, patients classified as high risk had a 2.8-fold higher risk of recurrence than those classified as low risk. The test also showed performance in two breast cancer types — triple-negative and HER2-positive — that currently have no reliable genomic test. The test relies on self-supervised pretraining rather than hand-labeled data alone, according to Yann LeCun, a Jacob T. Schwartz Chaired Professor and one of the paper’s authors. The work was led by Krzysztof J. Geras, co-founder and chief scientific officer of Ataraxis AI. The researchers said evaluation in completed randomized clinical trials is still needed before the test could guide treatment decisions. Several paper authors hold equity in Ataraxis AI, and NYU maintains financial and intellectual property interests in the company.

quickHits.headline: Pace University Nursing Students Conduct Independent Patient Interviews Using A.I. Avatars in Simulation Lab Pilot
quickHits.summary:
In Fall 2025, students in Pace University's Psychiatric Mental Health Nurse Practitioner Program were the first to pilot A.I.-enabled patient simulations. Under faculty leads Laura Kelly, PhD, and Gabrielle Ranger-Murdock, PhD, students used A.I. avatars to conduct independent interviews with multiple patients during a single "clinic day" — an activity the center's director, Nancy Owen, says is not possible with traditional simulation modalities. Students also practiced using screening instruments for anxiety, depression, and trauma, and worked on consultation skills through unfolding patient cases.

In the undergraduate nursing program, educators Aimee Smith and Nancy Harrison designed a pediatrics case featuring a nonverbal child, with the A.I. encounter built around interaction with the child's mother to develop guardian communication skills.

The A.I. platforms can evaluate student performance using faculty-developed rubrics that assess diagnostic accuracy and empathetic communication. Faculty begin with prebuilt simulations and adjust them to align with course objectives. Owen notes the technology is also reducing grading time.

Not every element has worked smoothly — Owen recalls one A.I. avatar that repeatedly addressed everyone as "honey." The center's standardized patient program, accredited through the Association of Standardized Patient Educators, continues alongside the A.I. simulations. "It's not replacing other modalities," Owen said. "It's enhancing our ability to design clinical encounters and measure competencies."

quickHits.headline: New America and ACCT Select Six Community Colleges for NSF-Backed Work-Based Learning Cohort
quickHits.summary:
Six community colleges have been selected for the Accelerator for Community Colleges in the Innovation Economy Work-Based Learning Capacity-Building Cohort, New America and the Association of Community College Trustees announced July 8. The cohort is offered through the Accelerator, a strategic initiative launched by New America and the U.S. National Science Foundation. The participating institutions are City Colleges of Chicago, East Central College (MO), Forsyth Technical Community College (NC), Santa Fe College (FL), SUNY Broome Community College (NY), and West Valley College (CA).

New America describes work-based learning as increasingly important as A.I. continues to reshape the labor market. Each cohort member will undertake a comprehensive institutional self-study, strategic planning, and implementation process using a toolkit developed jointly by New America and ACCT. Upon completing the process, cohort members will be recognized as pilot partners when the two organizations publish the toolkit for use by community colleges nationwide.

Colleges were selected based on demonstrated commitment to working with on-campus and off-campus stakeholders, existing employer and regional industry partnerships, and organizational capacity to complete the self-study process. Erwin Gianchandani, NSF Assistant Director for Technology, Innovation, and Partnerships, cited apprenticeships, internships, and work-based learning as preparation for jobs in artificial intelligence, microelectronics, biotech, and quantum technology, among other fields.

quickHits.headline: Survey of 1,947 Educators Across 36 Countries Finds Optimism — Not Alarm — About A.I. in Adult Learning
quickHits.summary:
Educators, trainers, and consultants worldwide are broadly optimistic about artificial intelligence in teaching and workforce development — and their primary concern is institutional support, not the technology itself. Those are the central findings of a survey administered by Singapore's Institute for Adult Learning, spanning 1,947 respondents across 36 countries, reported in an Auburn University news release this week.

The survey results appear in "Navigating the AI Frontier in Adult Education," an open-access book co-edited by Leslie Cordie, associate professor of adult education at Auburn University's Department of Educational Foundations, Leadership, and Technology, and published through Taylor & Francis.

Respondents largely viewed A.I. as a tool capable of improving teaching, reducing repetitive tasks, and creating new learning opportunities. Their biggest concern was not adopting the technology but receiving adequate guidance and institutional support to use it effectively.

Cordie herself uses A.I. to brainstorm research ideas, redesign course materials, create grading rubrics, and identify journals for publication. Rather than replacing her expertise, she said, the technology frees time for student conversations, collaboration, and deeper learning. "It's making me a better educator," Cordie said.

In her courses — which span workforce development, experiential learning, and comparative international education — Cordie asks students to experiment with A.I., question its outputs, and think critically about what it can and cannot do.

The book is available as an open-access title through Taylor & Francis.

quickHits.headline: Arizona Universities Build A.I. Curricula Around Judgment and Ethics Rather Than Technical Degrees
quickHits.summary: Grand Canyon University, the University of Arizona, and the University of Phoenix are each embedding A.I. ethics and critical thinking across existing coursework rather than racing to launch standalone technical programs, AZ Big Media reported. GCU President Brian Mueller described the institution's position plainly: "There's this race to establish technical AI degrees as soon as possible. We hope to use AI to supplement learning, not replace it." GCU operates four discipline-specific A.I. tutoring tools — Isaac for math, Mira for health sciences, Bloom for education exam prep, and Aiden for scenario-based learning — across more than 90 A.I.-integrated courses. Students are required to disclose A.I. use and are graded on how well they manage it. At the University of Arizona's College of Information Science, associate professor Diana Daly teaches students to identify bias by interacting directly with A.I. systems as users — for example, using translation prompts to surface gender bias in outputs. The college is launching an A.I. and society minor this fall. The University of Arizona has also established an Office of Responsible Artificial Intelligence. At the University of Phoenix, Vice President Leo Goncalves said the university began machine-learning work in 2021, before widespread A.I. adoption, and has since built a culture centered on validation and ethical use. "AI is not inherently good or bad," Goncalves said. "It's a force multiplier for whatever systems are already in existence."
